Let’s call it the **glass-ribbon** (*Cryonectes ammoniophilus*)—a speculative creature evolved in the cold, high-pressure ammonia seas of a dim red-dwarf planet.

### Environment
The ocean is liquid ammonia, roughly –55 °C, under several bars of pressure, with dissolved methane, hydrogen, nitrates, and organic tholins falling from the sky. Water is not the solvent here; it exists only as ice or as a waste product trapped in special glands. Light is dim and red. The sea is less viscous than water and has a sharp, pungent chemistry.

### Body Plan
The glass-ribbon is a long, flattened, ribbon-shaped animal, 2–3 meters long, 30–40 centimeters wide, and about 10 centimeters thick. It tapers to a point at the tail and has a blunt, bulbous head. Along its back runs a low dorsal ridge; along its belly, a keel. Six paddle-like limbs emerge from its sides—two near the head, two mid-body, two near the tail—used mainly for steering and slow rowing. Its tail is a broad vertical fluke.

### Skin and Skeleton
Its skin is a flexible, chitinous cuticle rather than fish scales. It is semi-translucent, bluish-white, and iridescent from thin films of ammonium salts. Beneath the skin lies a hydrostatic skeleton: fluid-filled chambers and cartilage-like rods. The creature adjusts buoyancy by shifting ammonia in and out of internal bladders. Its skin is dotted with pores for chemoreception and gas exchange.

### Internal Chemistry
Inside, its solvent is liquid ammonia. Its cells are built from polyamide-like membranes and amide-linked genetic polymers unlike Earth DNA. Its enzymes are metal-centered polyamides that function at cryogenic temperatures. Its circulatory fluid is a pale blue ammonia-based blood carrying copper-iron complexes that transport dissolved hydrogen and nitrate. A simple heart pumps this fluid through a network of vessels.

### Metabolism and Respiration
It does not breathe oxygen. It is a chemosynthetic heterotroph. Its long coiled gut grazes on “ammonia snow”—organic tholin particles—and scrapes chemosynthetic mats around vents. Symbiotic microbes in its gut use dissolved hydrogen to reduce nitrate to ammonia, releasing energy. The host uses that ammonia for solvent and nitrogen. Water produced as a byproduct is concentrated in ice glands and expelled as tiny ice crystals. Feathery gill lamellae along its dorsal ridge absorb hydrogen and nitrate and release nitrogen gas.

### Senses and Communication
It has four eyes on short stalks: two large forward-facing eyes for binocular vision, and two smaller dorsal eyes for shadow detection. They see in deep red and near-infrared, suited to its dim red sun. A lateral line of sensitive cilia runs along its flanks, detecting vibrations and currents. Chemoreceptive pits cover its head and tentacles, letting it taste the ammonia sea for food, mates, and predators. It can produce low clicks with pharyngeal plates and hear echoes through its lower jaw. It also senses weak electric fields. Its skin can flush red or blue for communication, and light organs along its sides emit faint blue-green bioluminescence.

### Behavior
The glass-ribbon is a slow, deliberate drifter. It swims by undulating its body in gentle waves, using its paddle-limbs for fine control. It can jet backward by contracting a mantle cavity and expelling ammonia through a ventral siphon. It is usually solitary but gathers in loose pods at vent fields. It is curious and may approach submersibles. When threatened, it curls into a tight spiral, exposing dorsal spines coated with toxic ammonium cyanide. It can also release a cloud of noxious chemicals and autotomize a limb to escape.

It is a hermaphrodite. During the “warm” season, adults gather in shallows and exchange packets of genetic material through tentacles. Eggs are laid in gelatinous strings attached to ice rocks or vent chimneys. Larvae are one-millimeter planktonic creatures with ciliated bands and a single eye. They drift for months, feeding on ammonia snow. If food is scarce, they can encyst for years. Metamorphosis into the adult form takes several molts. Lifespan is 80–100 Earth years.

It is a mid-level consumer and a nitrogen cycler. It is preyed upon by hook-mouthed siphon predators and ice-skimming skaters. Its body provides shelter for parasitic ammonia mites and commensal gill worms. Its ice glands may leave tiny ice trails that other creatures follow.

Its skin would feel cold and slippery, not wet, because liquid ammonia has low surface tension. Its smell would be pungent—ammonia mixed with burnt sugar. Ammoneustes is a filter-feeder, scavenger, and occasional predator. Its tentacles sweep ammonoplankton from the current; its radula-like tongue scrapes microbial mats from ice rocks. Its chemistry would be built around ammonia rather than water, its senses tuned to a dark, chemical world, and its life strategy one of patience, chemosynthesis, and long, cold endurance. **Overall form.**  
The Glass Ribbon is a ribbon-like organism, 8 to 12 meters long, 1 meter wide, and only half a meter thick. Its body is flattened and translucent, so the dark ammonia sea glows faintly through it. The skin is not soft like jelly; it is covered by a thin, slippery cuticle of waxy amides and ether-linked lipids, giving it a wet, pearly sheen. Along its edges, thin films of crystalline salts and proteins create faint iridescent blues and greens. It has no bones. Instead, it maintains its shape with a hydrostatic skeleton: dozens of fluid-filled chambers running the length of its body, pressurized with ammonia-based hemolymph.

The anterior end is a rounded hood. Beneath the hood is a ventral mouth surrounded by eight short, muscular tentacles used for grazing and manipulating food. Two much longer feeding tentacles can extend three meters to snare small swimmers or gather ammonia snow. The Glass Ribbon has no eyes in the human sense. A dorsal patch of photosensitive tissue detects the faint bioluminescence of other creatures, and its own body carries symbiotic glowing bacteria in small sacs along its flanks. It flashes in slow, rippling patterns to communicate with others of its kind.

The Glass Ribbon swims by undulating its body in gentle waves, using a dorsal fin and a ventral membrane for steering. Because liquid ammonia is less viscous than water, it can glide with less effort, but it must be careful not to overshoot. For emergencies, it has a muscular siphon at its tail. By contracting its rear chambers, it can jet a stream of ammonia and accelerate rapidly away from danger. To keep from sinking, it maintains a series of internal gas bladders filled with hydrogen and methane produced by symbiotic microbes. By adjusting the gas volume, it can hover at different depths, from the sunlit upper ammonia layer to the cold, crushing darkness below.

**Internal systems.**  
Its body fluids are liquid ammonia carrying dissolved ammonium salts, cryoprotectants, and proteins. Its “blood” is not red but a pale blue, using a copper-based pigment to transport sulfur and hydrogen compounds. It has a simple tubular heart that beats only once every ten seconds. Its nerves are slow, but its reactions are deliberate rather than sluggish. The digestive tract begins at the mouth, passes through a crop, a midgut, and a large digestive gland. Symbiotic bacteria in the gut break down complex hydrocarbons and organic snow into simpler molecules. The creature does not breathe oxygen; instead, it absorbs dissolved nitrogen compounds through its skin and gills, using nitrate and nitrite as electron acceptors in a slow, cold-adapted metabolism. Its cells use ether-linked lipids and amide-rich proteins, and its genetic material is a peptide-nucleic-acid-like polymer, stable in the presence of ammonia.

**Diet and behavior.**  
The Glass Ribbon is an omnivorous filterer and grazer. It sweeps its tentacles through clouds of ammonia snow, consuming organic particles, tiny planktonic larvae, and the occasional small swimmer. It can also scavenge carcasses on the ammonia seafloor. It is generally solitary, but during the long winter it gathers in slow-moving spirals of dozens of individuals. They communicate with bioluminescent pulses and chemical signals released into the ammonia. When threatened, it can curl into a tight spiral to protect its head, autotomize a tail segment to distract a predator, or release a cloud of noxious amines and ammonium chloride that irritates sensitive chemoreceptors.

The Glass Ribbon is hermaphroditic. Adults release gametes into the ammonia currents during seasonal blooms of organic snow. The larvae are tiny, ciliated, and planktonic, drifting for several years before metamorphosing into juvenile ribbons. Old individuals become more translucent and their bioluminescence dims, until they finally sink to the seafloor and are consumed by scavengers.

In the ammonia ocean, the Glass Ribbon is both grazer and prey. It helps control the drifting organic snow and cycles nitrogen and sulfur through the ecosystem. Larger predators—siphon-jetted hunters with crystalline jaws—hunt it, while smaller parasites attach to its skin. Its gas bladders and glowing symbionts also support a miniature ecosystem of microbes and tiny crustacean-like swimmers that live on and inside it.

To human eyes, the Glass Ribbon would seem alien and fragile, a ghostly ribbon drifting through a sea that would freeze water into stone. In that ocean drifts a creature about four meters long, shaped like a cross between a ribbon eel and a siphonophore. Its common name is the glacier ghost.

**Body plan.**  
The glacier ghost has three main regions: a dorsal float, a long central trunk, and a trailing cluster of six feeding tentacles. The dorsal float is a gas-filled sac containing a methane-hydrogen mixture. By squeezing muscles around the sac, the creature can expand or compress it, adjusting its buoyancy so it hovers at different depths. The trunk is flattened side to side, with two undulating lateral fins that ripple like slow wings. The tentacles can trail six meters behind it, each covered in fine chemoreceptive hairs and tiny harpoon-like spicules.

Its skin is translucent and iridescent, laced with microscopic crystals of ammonia clathrate that reflect sound. Beneath the skin lies a layer of ammonia-clathrate foam, which traps gas in tiny cages and insulates the body from the cold. The creature has no bones of calcium. Instead, it uses a hydrostatic skeleton: fluid-filled chambers of liquid ammonia stiffened by cartilage-like struts of a chitin-ammonia polymer. Its mouth is armed with a beak of water ice, reinforced with ammonia clathrate, which it sharpens by gnawing on frozen water rocks on the seafloor.

**Internal physiology.**  
The glacier ghost is not water-based. Its cells are filled with liquid ammonia, salted with ammonium chloride, methanol, and ethane to keep from freezing near vents or during cold upwellings. Its genetic material is a peptide-nucleic-acid analogue, stable in ammonia and resistant to ammonolysis. Its membranes are built from long fluorinated lipids, which are “ammoniaphobic” and keep the body’s solvent from leaking into the sea.

It has an open circulatory system. Pale blue-green hemolymph is pumped by a simple heart-like organ, carrying dissolved gases and nutrients. The nervous system is a ventral nerve cord with a small brain around the esophagus. Signals travel as ammonium-ion gradients rather than sodium-potassium gradients. It breathes through gill-like ammonobranchs that exchange dissolved hydrogen, methane, and nitrogen with the ocean.

**Senses and behavior.**  
Light is scarce, so the glacier ghost relies mostly on sound and chemistry. It produces low-frequency clicks from a sonar organ in its forehead and listens for echoes with a lower jaw shaped like a parabolic dish. Two rows of chemoreceptive pits run along its flanks, tasting the water for amines, nitriles, and dissolved organics. Electroreceptive ampullae detect the weak fields of prey. Simple eyespots can detect bioluminescent flashes, but they are secondary.

It is a slow drifter, often moving in vertical migrations that follow chemical plumes from hydrothermal vents. When threatened, it contracts its trunk and jets ammonia through a ventral siphon, then releases a cloud of ammonia-clathrate particles that scatters sonar and confuses predators. It also communicates with low, resonant rumbles that travel for kilometers through the dense ammonia sea.

The glacier ghost is an omnivorous grazer and filter feeder. It sweeps its tentacles through clouds of ammonoplankton—tiny drifting organisms—and scrapes mats of ammonophytes from vent chimneys. Its gut hosts symbiotic microbes that use hydrogen from vents and acetylene from the atmosphere as an energy source. These microbes oxidize hydrogen and reduce acetylene to ethylene, generating energy-rich compounds that feed the host. The creature also absorbs some nutrients directly through its skin.

It is a hermaphrodite. During seasonal upwellings, adults release gametes into the currents. Fertilized eggs develop into ciliated larvae that drift as plankton for weeks. The larvae eventually settle near hydrothermal vents, where they metamorphose into juveniles. Adults can live for decades, growing slowly in the cold.

**Ecology.**  
The glacier ghost is a mid-level consumer. It is preyed upon by ice-jawed predators—creatures with jaws of crystalline water ice—and by larger colonial drifters. It hosts parasites and provides shelter for small commensal organisms that live in its tentacle cluster. When it dies, its body sinks and becomes a feast for scavengers, returning nitrogen and carbon to the ammonia ocean.

**Why it works.**  
In a world where ammonia is the solvent, life cannot use water-based biochemistry. The glacier ghost solves this by using ammonia-based cells, fluorinated membranes, PNA-like genes, and chemosynthetic symbionts. Its gas float lets it navigate a less dense ocean. Its sonar and chemoreception replace vision. Its ice beak turns the frozen water of its world into a tool. It is not a fish, not a jellyfish, but something wholly alien—a cold, drifting ghost of an ammonia sea.

CREATURE DESCRIPTION:
**Field notes: *Nyxammon vitreus*, the ammonia drifter**

*Assumptions: a cold, high-pressure world where ammonia is liquid at the surface—roughly −55 °C and 8–10 bar under a thick hydrogen/nitrogen atmosphere. The oceans are mostly liquid ammonia with dissolved salts, amides, and organic molecules; water is rare and biologically troublesome.*

The ammonia drifter is a slow, translucent predator that looks like a cross between a nautilus, a jellyfish, and a deep-sea squid. It is about three meters long and mass perhaps 150–250 kg, most of that a central buoyancy shell. Its body is pale blue-white, faintly iridescent, and semi-transparent enough that its internal organs appear as dark, shifting shadows.

**Body plan.** At the front is a tapered, flexible shell made not of calcium carbonate but of a chitin-like polysaccharide cross-linked with nitrogen-rich proteins. The shell is divided into gas chambers filled with hydrogen and methane, which the creature produces metabolically. By pumping ammonium ions into and out of the chamber fluids, it changes the gas volume and therefore its depth. Six long tentacles trail behind it, lined with fine silica spicules and sticky ammonogel. Four broad lateral fins run along the flanks, undulating slowly for steering. A siphon beneath the shell can expel a jet of ammonia for quick escape.

**Skin and skeleton.** Its outer integument, the ammonioderm, is a multi-layered membrane built from ammonia-compatible lipids: polar ammonium-headed molecules facing the ammonia ocean, nonpolar tails facing inward. Beneath that lies a hydraulic body cavity filled with liquid ammonia carrying ammonium salts, amides, and dissolved gases. It has no bones; support comes from silica spicules and tough polyamide fibers, giving it a rubbery, jointed flexibility.

**Metabolism.** The drifter is not water-based. Its cells use liquid ammonia as solvent, and its “blood” is a cold, faintly conductive ammonia solution. It breathes dissolved hydrogen and nitrate, combining them in a slow redox reaction that yields energy, nitrogen gas, and water. Water is a waste product and a potential toxin because it dilutes the ammonia solvent. The creature therefore shunts water into specialized glands, crystallizes it, and sheds it as tiny frost scales that drift away like snow. Its metabolism is extremely slow; a meal can sustain it for weeks, and its lifespan may exceed a century.

**Senses.** It has no image-forming eyes. Instead, rows of chemoreceptive pits along its tentacles taste the water for amino acids, sulfur compounds, and ammonium gradients. Thermoreceptors detect the faint warmth of hydrothermal plumes. A lateral-line system senses pressure waves and currents, and it can generate weak electric fields through ammonium-ion pumps, using them to detect nearby prey and obstacles. Along its fins are bioluminescent photophores that pulse blue-green, used for communication and possibly to lure small swimmers.

**Feeding.** The drifter is an opportunistic predator and scavenger. It trails its tentacles through clouds of “cryoplankton”—microscopic ammonia-based autotrophs—and small shrimp-like swimmers. When prey touches a tentacle, sticky ammonogel and tiny silica harpoons hold it fast. The tentacle retracts to a central mouth, where the creature ejects digestive enzymes into a muscular pouch. Digestion happens externally in this pouch, breaking prey into ammonium salts and soluble organics that are absorbed through a ruffled gut lining. Indigestible fragments are expelled as dense pellets that sink.

**Reproduction and life cycle.** It is a hermaphrodite. During the brief “summer” when ocean temperatures rise toward −45 °C, adults release sperm packets and gelatinous egg cases. Eggs are anchored in crevices of ammonia ice or on the seafloor. The larvae are planktonic, ciliated, and only a few millimeters long. The Ammoniath lives on **Nerith**, a moon orbiting a gas giant. Its atmosphere is thick and cold—about 4 bar, mostly nitrogen, methane, hydrogen, and argon. The ocean is liquid ammonia at roughly **−55 °C**, with dissolved ammonium chloride, ammonium cyanide, nitrates, phosphates, and traces of acetylene and hydrazine. Sunlight is dim and red. At the bottom, **cryovents** release warmth, hydrogen, methane, and mineral salts. Because solid ammonia is denser than liquid ammonia, any ice that forms sinks, so the seafloor is littered with ammonia-ice gravel rather than floating icebergs.

### Form
An adult Ammoniath is about **3–4 meters long** and a meter thick, shaped like a cross between a sea cucumber and a squid. Its body is a segmented, translucent cylinder, milky blue with faint internal organs visible through the skin. Six lateral fin-wings undulate slowly for steering, while a ventral mat of cilia helps it creep over bacterial mats. At the front is a rounded **sensory turret** studded with chemical pits, thermal organs, and electroreceptors. At the rear is a muscular **siphon** used for jet propulsion and sound production. Its skin, called **cryoderm**, is a flexible armor of cross-linked amides and nitriles, embedded with tiny ammonium-carbamate crystals. It feels like cold, wet leather.

### Anatomy
Internally, the Ammoniath has a hydrostatic skeleton reinforced by **ammochitin** rods—an ammonia-stable polymer similar to chitin. Its muscles are slow but powerful, built from amide-based contractile fibers that work efficiently at low temperatures. Two dorsal gas bladders filled with nitrogen and methane let it hover at different depths.

It feeds through a mouth surrounded by feathery tentacles and a rasping radula. Food passes into a crop and then a midgut, but much of its energy comes from a spongy organ called the **trophosome**. This organ houses symbiotic bacteria that oxidize hydrogen using nitrate or nitrite, releasing nitrogen gas and water, or that hydrogenate acetylene into ethane. The host supplies the bacteria with hydrogen, nitrate, and ammonia; in return, it receives carbon compounds and energy. The Ammoniath also grazes on ammonoplankton and bacterial mats.

Circulation is open. Its hemolymph is liquid ammonia carrying dissolved nutrients and a copper-based pigment, **ammocyanin**, which helps move electrons and nitrogen oxides. Respiration occurs through external frilly gills called **ammonobranchs**, which absorb dissolved gases and ions and release nitrogen and methane. The nervous system is a ring of ganglia around the esophagus, plus a diffuse nerve net. Signals travel via ammonium-ion gradients and amino-acid neurotransmitters. It is not fast, but it is capable of complex behavior.

The Ammoniath is ammonia-based. Its cellular solvent is liquid ammonia, and its energy currency uses **phosphoramidate bonds**—an ammonia-world analogue of ATP. Its genetic material is **ANA** (ammonia nucleic acid), a peptide-nucleic-acid-like molecule with an amide backbone and nitrogenous bases. Membranes are made of long-chain amides and ammonium head groups, held together by hydrogen bonds and ionic interactions rather than strong hydrophobic forces. It also produces antifreeze glycoproteins and high salt concentrations to prevent ammonia ice from forming in its tissues.

The Ammoniath has no true eyes. Instead, it senses the world through:

- **Mechanoreception:** a lateral-line system detects currents, vibrations, and the approach of predators.
- **Electroreception:** ampullae detect weak bioelectric fields from prey and other Ammoniaths.
- **Echolocation:** it clicks through its siphon and listens with a sonar bulb in its brain.
- **Photoreception:** simple eyespots detect the pale blue bioluminescence it produces by chemiluminescent oxidation of hydrazine. It uses these flashes to signal others and lure prey.

The Ammoniath is a peaceful grazer and scavenger. It migrates vertically, following chemical plumes to cryovents, where it “recharges” its symbiotic bacteria. When threatened, it jets away and releases a cloud of ammonia-ice crystals and noxious ammonium cyanide to confuse predators. It lives in loose herds around vent fields, communicating with low clicks and light flashes.

Ammoniaths are hermaphroditic. During periods of cryovolcanic activity, they release gametes into the vent plumes. The larvae are planktonic, ciliated, and have simple eyespots. After one to two years, they settle near vents and metamorphose into adults. They can live **50–100 Earth years**, and if the ocean freezes, they can enter a dormant “cryobiotic” state in the sediment.

In its ecosystem, the Ammoniath is a key grazer and a major prey item for larger ammonia-ocean predators. Its symbionts help cycle nitrogen, converting nitrate into nitrogen gas, and its body provides shelter and nutrients for several smaller ammonia-adapted organisms. *Cryonectes ammoniensis* — “the ghost ray of the ammonia sea”

**Environment.** Imagine a cold world orbiting a dim red star. Its atmosphere is thick with hydrogen, methane, nitrogen, and haze. The ocean below is liquid ammonia at about 210 K (–63 °C), kept liquid by pressure and dissolved salts. Because solid ammonia is denser than liquid ammonia, ice does not float; it sinks. There is no familiar ice ceiling, only a dark, faintly violet sea lit by bioluminescence and the occasional shaft of red starlight.

**Overall form.** The ammoniid is a large, flattened pelagic creature, roughly 3 meters across and 2 meters long, weighing about 200 kilograms. It looks like a cross between a manta ray and a cuttlefish: a diamond-shaped body, six wing-like fins, and a fan-shaped tail. Its skin is semi-translucent and deep indigo, with clusters of blue-green bioluminescent spots along its fins. Because its tissues have almost the same refractive index as liquid ammonia, it appears ghostly and half-dissolved when seen from a distance.

**Skin and skeleton.** Its outer surface is covered by a waxy tholin cuticle that limits ammonia loss and insulates it from the cold. Beneath that is a dermis packed with ammonia-filled vacuoles and natural antifreeze compounds—methanol, methylamine, and specialized glycoproteins—that keep its internal fluids from freezing. It has no true bone. Instead, its body is supported by flexible chitin-protein struts and pressurized ammonia bladders, giving it a rubbery, resilient frame.

**Internal systems.** The ammoniid has two hearts and a closed circulatory system. Its blood is ammonia-based, pale blue, and carries a copper-nickel complex for electron transport. It breathes through gills along its flanks, absorbing dissolved hydrogen, methane, acetylene, and nitrate from the ocean. Its metabolism is anaerobic and chemosynthetic: it oxidizes hydrogen and simple hydrocarbons using nitrate and metal ions, releasing nitrogen gas and amides. Water, a waste product, freezes immediately at ocean temperature and is either stored as tiny ice granules or expelled as ballast.

**Nervous system and senses.** Its brain is a ring of ganglia around the esophagus. It is not fast by Earth standards, but it is efficient, with giant axons that trigger rapid escape bursts. It senses the world through several channels:
- **Echolocation:** clicks produced in a fatty melon-like organ, used to map the dark sea. Sound travels well in liquid ammonia.
- **Lateral line:** detects currents, pressure changes, and the wake of prey.
- **Chemoreception:** tentacles around its mouth taste dissolved amino acids, nitriles, and metal ions.
- **Vision:** large, sensitive eyes tuned to red light and bioluminescence; it sees poorly in bright light but excels in gloom.
- **Electroreception:** detects weak electric fields from living cells and moving muscles.

**Locomotion.** It swims by undulating its body and flapping its six fins, sometimes jetting ammonia through a siphon for a sudden burst. Normal cruising speed is about 2 meters per second; a frightened ammoniid can reach 5 m/s. It controls buoyancy with hydrogen-filled bladders, which also help it avoid sinking ammonia ice.

**Diet and ecology.** The ammoniid is an omnivorous filter-feeder and scavenger. It cruises with its mouth open, straining “ammonia plankton”—chemoautotrophic microbes that oxidize hydrogen and nitrates—through chitinous baleen. It also feeds on tholin snow falling from the upper ocean and on carrion. In turn, it is hunted by larger, deeper-dwelling predators, so it defends itself by releasing a cloud of noxious amines and flashing confusing bioluminescent patterns.

**Reproduction and life cycle.** It reproduces sexually, with internal fertilization. Females lay three to five leathery eggs in warm hydrothermal vent fields, where the ammonia is slightly warmer and richer in dissolved minerals. The larvae are planktonic for five to ten years before metamorphosing into juveniles. Growth is slow, maturity takes decades, and individuals may live 200 to 400 Earth years.

**Biochemistry.** This creature is not water-based. Its cells use liquid ammonia as solvent. Its enzymes—“ammoniazymes”—rely on different ionic bridges and hydrophobic pockets than Earth enzymes. Its membranes are not ordinary lipid bilayers; they are “ammonosomes” made of branched isoprenoid chains with amide headgroups, stabilized against ammonia’s solvent power. Its genetic material is an ammonia-stable polymer analogous to DNA, sometimes called ANA, with an amide-linked backbone and nitrogen-rich bases.

**Behavior.** Ammoniids live in small pods, communicating through low-frequency sound and rhythmic bioluminescent flashes. They migrate vertically with tidal heating and follow chemical plumes from vents. They are curious but cautious, and they often gather around geothermal springs where the ammonia ocean is warmest and life is densest.

If you dropped one into Earth’s ocean, it would die almost instantly: its ammonia blood would boil or freeze, its membranes would destabilize, and its biochemistry would collapse. But in its own cold, dark ammonia sea, the ghost ray would be a slow, elegant, and perfectly adapted native.

The body cavity is filled with liquid ammonia, which serves as both hydrostatic skeleton and circulatory fluid. A simple peristaltic heart pushes the ammolymph through a network of open sinuses. Respiration occurs through large, frilly gills housed in chambers behind the head. Ammonia is a basic solvent with a lower dielectric constant and weaker hydrogen bonding than water. Its membranes are not ordinary lipid bilayers but layered lipoamide sheets stabilized by hydrogen bonds and ammonium-ion bridges. The ice-worm “tastes” the sea with thousands of chemoreceptors on its tentacles, detecting amino acids, nitriles, and metal ions at trace concentrations. It swims by undulating its six fins and tail, and can jet by expelling ammonia from a siphon. Cruising speed is about 1–2 km/h; a startled burst might reach 10 km/h. It is not fast, but it is persistent.

CREATURE DESCRIPTION:
**The Ammonia Wraith** (*Nyxovenator crystallinus*)

Imagine a cold super-Earth called Kaldra, orbiting a dim red dwarf. Its oceans are not water but liquid ammonia, kept fluid at about –55°C by a thick nitrogen-methane atmosphere at 8 bars of pressure. The sea is dark, slightly less dense than water, and rich in dissolved ammonium salts, hydrazine, methane, and complex organic molecules. In this alien ocean swims the Ammonia Wraith—a ghostly, bioluminescent predator perfectly adapted to a world where water is a mineral and ammonia is the solvent of life.

### Size and Shape
The Ammonia Wraith is about 5 meters long and a meter wide at its thickest, massing around 250 kilograms. It looks like a cross between a deep-sea squid and a moray eel: a long, flexible torpedo of a body covered by a translucent, iridescent mantle. Its outer skin is a composite of ammonia-clathrate crystals and a chitin-like polymer, giving it a glassy, armored appearance while remaining flexible. Six lateral fins run along its flanks, and a fan-shaped tail provides thrust. Two long, retractable feeding tentacles extend from beneath its head, and a muscular siphon near the neck allows it to jet ammonia for rapid lunges or escapes.

### Coloration and Bioluminescence
The creature is pale blue-green, nearly invisible in the gloom. Rows of bioluminescent photophores line its flanks and tentacles, pulsing in cold chemical light—violet, blue, and green. These lights are used for communication, luring prey, and startling predators. The glow is produced by a luciferin/luciferase system that functions in liquid ammonia, not water.

### Internal Anatomy
- **Skeleton:** No bones. It relies on a hydrostatic skeleton of ammonia-filled vesicles and a flexible cartilage-like material made of cross-linked proteins. This lets it squeeze through narrow ice crevices and undulate gracefully.
- **Circulatory system:** An open circulatory system. Its “blood” is liquid ammonia carrying dissolved nutrients, ammonium ions, and a copper-based pigment called ammonocyanin, which gives it a faint blue tint. A series of muscular pumps along the dorsal vessel circulates it.
- **Respiration:** Feathery gills absorb nitrate and trace hydrogen from the surrounding ammonia. It uses nitrate as an electron acceptor, reducing it to nitrogen gas, which it exhales through its siphon. This anaerobic respiration is slow but efficient in the cold.
- **Digestion:** A sharp beak made of scleroprotein and a radula tear prey apart. The midgut is filled with ammonia-based enzymes and symbiotic bacteria that break down proteins, lipids, and carbohydrates. Waste nitrogen is excreted as ammonium salts.
- **Buoyancy:** Along its dorsal line are methane-filled sacs. By adjusting the methane pressure, it can hover at different depths without swimming.
- **Nervous system:** A dorsal nerve cord and a cluster of ganglia in the head. Its neurons are large and use ammonium ion gradients. Signals travel slowly, but the wraith is patient and ambush-oriented. A decentralized nerve net in its fins allows quick reflexes.

### Senses
- **Echolocation:** It produces low-frequency clicks from a sonic organ near the siphon. Sound travels well in liquid ammonia. It receives echoes through acoustic membranes along its head and flanks, building a detailed mental map of its surroundings.
- **Electroreception:** Ammonia has a low dielectric constant, so electric fields from prey’s nerve and muscle activity propagate farther than in water. The wraith has ampullae along its jaw and tentacles to detect these fields.
- **Chemoreception:** Its skin and tentacles are covered with chemoreceptors that taste the ammonia solution for traces of blood, pheromones, and prey.
- **Vision:** Two small, dark-adapted eyes detect bioluminescence and the faint red glow of hydrothermal vents.
- **Touch:** Sensitive cilia detect pressure waves and currents.

### Behavior
The Ammonia Wraith is an ambush predator. It hovers motionless, using its methane sacs to maintain depth. When prey approaches, it jets ammonia from its siphon and shoots forward, grabbing with its tentacles. Its beak crushes shells and exoskeletons. It also scavenges.

It communicates with complex bioluminescent patterns and low-frequency clicks. Different patterns indicate aggression, courtship, or alarm. When threatened, it ejects a cloud of “ammonia ink”—a mixture of ammonium chloride and long-chain amines. In the cold ammonia, this crystallizes into a dense, blinding snow that confuses predators. It can also autotomize a fin or tail segment to escape.

Mostly solitary, it gathers in small pods during mating season or at rich feeding grounds.

### Reproduction and Life Cycle
Separate sexes. During the warm season, when ammonia currents bring nutrients, males transfer spermatophores to females. Females lay gelatinous clutches of eggs on rocks or ice shelves. The eggs have tough, ammonia-insoluble shells.

Larvae are planktonic, transparent, and ciliated. They feed on chemosynthetic bacteria and drift with currents for about two years. Then they metamorphose into juveniles, developing fins, tentacles, and bioluminescent organs. Lifespan is 100–200 Earth years. They grow slowly and can enter torpor during ammonia storms or when food is scarce.

### Ecology
The Ammonia Wraith is a keystone predator in the Kaldran ammonia ocean. It controls populations of smaller grazers and filter-feeders. Its carcass falls to the abyssal zone, where chemosynthetic communities consume it. Its symbiotic gut bacteria fix nitrogen, enriching the ocean with bioavailable nitrogen. It migrates vertically, following prey and nutrient upwellings. It is preyed upon by larger “ammonia leviathans” and occasionally by pack-hunting “cryo-sharks.”

### Biochemistry
Its cells use liquid ammonia as solvent. Cell membranes are made of ammonolipids—polar head groups that dissolve in ammonia and branched hydrocarbon tails that stay fluid at –55°C. Proteins have extra disulfide bonds and metal cofactors to stabilize their shape in the weaker hydrogen-bonding environment. Its genetic material is a double helix of “ammono-DNA,” a polymer with an amide backbone and different base pairs. Metabolism is slow; a single meal can last for weeks.

In short, the Ammonia Wraith is a ghostly, bioluminescent predator of a cold, alien sea—a creature perfectly adapted to a world where water is a mineral and ammonia is the stuff of life.
